claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by synchronized reduction and concomitant nucleation of all metal precursors.
Synchronous reduction and nucleation kinetically trap a homogeneous mixture of metals.
Kinetic trapping prevents phase separation and elemental segregation.
Significantly different precursor-reduction rates cause phase separation or elemental segregation.
The reaction environment can be adjusted to balance precursor-reduction kinetics and make atomic nucleation concurrent.
Coupling between reduction, nucleation, and subsequent atomic diffusion determines whether a well-mixed alloy or phase-separated domains form.
Balanced reduction kinetics cause all metal species to reach the nucleation threshold simultaneously.
Simultaneous nucleation forms a locked-in uniform alloy phase before significant diffusion or segregation occurs.
Under asynchronous reduction, early-reducing species nucleate first and bias the local composition.
The local-composition bias caused by early nucleation promotes phase separation or elemental segregation.
Tuned conditions will produce nanoparticles with a homogeneous alloy structure, uniform elemental distribution, and minimal phase boundaries.
An unchanged baseline will produce nanoparticles with phase separation or elemental inhomogeneity.
Standard synthesis parameters that do not target equalized reduction kinetics typically result in sequential nucleation and heterogeneity.
The mechanism should apply to noble-metal systems whose differences in reduction potentials are moderate enough to be balanced through reaction tuning.
The mechanism may not apply when constituent reduction potentials are extremely disparate.
Extremely high temperatures or rapid solvent evaporation may override control of reduction kinetics and place the synthesis outside the proposed mechanism's scope.
Ligand effects and solvent interactions may shift the conditions required for synchronized reduction.
Failure of tuned conditions to improve compositional homogeneity and alloy-phase uniformity relative to the unchanged baseline would falsify the proposed governing role of synchronous reduction.
